literal: Official Posts Treatise, Part One
idiomatic: Official Posts Treatise I

literal: Offices arise from duties; duties follow from affairs; and names are imposed upon them.
idiomatic: Offices grow out of duties, duties from tasks, and names are layered on top.

literal: Later ages inherit the names without investigating the substance.
idiomatic: Later generations kept the titles without asking what they actually did.

literal: The Ministry of Personnel—once the Grand Steward—became Grand Minister of Education, became Director of the Department of State Affairs, became Secretariat Director, became Gate-of-the-Sons Chancellery;
idiomatic: Personnel had been Grand Steward, then Grand Minister of Education, Secretariat Director, and Gate Chancellery;

literal: The Ministry of War—once the Minister of War—became Grand Minister of War, became Grand Marshal, became Privy Commissioner.
idiomatic: War had been Minister of War, then Grand Minister of War, Grand Marshal, and Privy Commissioner.

literal: Inheriting ancient office names, they matched present duties to them; thus the former kings' methods for ordering all under Heaven, like sorting silk that is already tangled, names and substance were confused.
idiomatic: Later regimes kept ancient titles and mapped current duties onto them, so the old way of governing the realm became like untangling snarled silk—name and reality mixed together.

literal: Khitan old custom: affairs were simple and duties exclusive; office institutions were plain and solid, not disturbed by names; their rise was swift indeed.
idiomatic: In Khitan custom affairs were few and posts focused; government was plain and did not trade on empty titles, and their rise was swift.

literal: In the sixth year of Taizu's Shence reign an edict rectified court ranks.
idiomatic: In Taizu Shence year 6 ranks at court were fixed by edict.

literal: By Taizong's time he also administered China; offices were divided into Northern and Southern faces, governing Khitan by national institutions and treating Han by Han institutions.
idiomatic: Under Taizong the state also ruled Chinese territory; offices split into Northern and Southern branches—Khitan governed by Liao law, Han by Han law.

literal: National institutions were simple and plain; in Han institutions the habit of inheriting names still remained.
idiomatic: The native system stayed spare; within the Chinese system the habit of nominal inheritance persisted.

literal: Liao state offices were divided into Northern and Southern Courts: the Northern Face governed palace accounts, tribes, and subject states; the Southern Face governed Han prefectures and counties, taxes, and military horses.
idiomatic: Liao offices split into Northern and Southern Courts—the north handled palace accounts, tribes, and subject peoples; the south handled Han districts, revenue, and cavalry.

literal: Governing according to custom, they obtained what was fitting.
idiomatic: Each branch ruled in its own way, which suited the realm.

literal: At first Taizu divided the Dieci yilijin into Northern and Southern Great Kings, called the Northern and Southern Courts.
idiomatic: Taizu first split the Dieci yilijin into Northern and Southern Great Kings—the Northern and Southern Courts.

literal: Chancellors, Privy Council, Xuanhui, linya, down to langjun and guards—all were divided into Northern and Southern, yet in substance all governed Northern Face affairs; those who speak of Liao offices need not be confused.
idiomatic: Chancellor, Privy Council, xuanhui, linya, langjun, and guards all had north and south posts, but in practice they handled northern affairs; commentators on Liao offices should not be misled by the labels.

literal: In general Liao offices: the Northern Privy Council corresponded to the Ministry of War, the Southern Privy Council to the Ministry of Personnel, the Northern and Southern Great Kings to the Ministry of Revenue, yilibi to the Ministry of Justice, xuanhui to the Ministry of Works, dilie mada to the Ministry of Rites, and the Northern and Southern Chancellors presided over all.
idiomatic: Broadly, Northern Privy Council stood for War, Southern Privy for Personnel, the two Great Kings for Revenue, yilibi for Justice, xuanhui for Works, dilie mada for Rites, with Northern and Southern Chancellors above them.

literal: Tithen governed the clans; linya revised documents and proclamations; yuyue sat to discuss policy, representing the duke and tutor at court.
idiomatic: Tithen oversaw the imperial clan, linya drafted state papers, and yuyue deliberated from his seat as a notional chief mentor at court.

literal: Affairs simple and duties focused—this is why Liao rose.
idiomatic: Simple tasks and focused posts were how Liao prospered.

literal: Through the Liao dynasty only three men gained the yuyue name for weight: Yelü Helu, Wuzhi, and Renxian—called the Three Yuyue.

idiomatic: In Xingzong Chongxi year 21 Yelü Yixian became tithen and warned the clan: "The Three Fathers' lines are the highest nobility and the source of public morals—no unfilial or unjust act, however slight, is permissible."

idiomatic: The Three Sovereigns were sages; even in the plainest age, night watches at the gates were stricter than indulging intruders.

literal: Liao's forebears had no walled cities, moats, or solid palaces; felt carts were camps and hard stockades were palaces—Imperial Account offices had to be strict.
idiomatic: Before cities and palaces, Liao ancestors camped in carts and fortified felt enclosures—so account-guard posts had to be rigorous.

literal: Noble kin served as attendants; those registered to the account were close attendants; Northern and Southern tribes were guards; military men were night guards; personal troops were forbidden guards; officials of the hundred offices took turns as night duty.
idiomatic: Kin of rank became attendants, account registrants close attendants, north and south tribes guards, warriors night guards, household troops forbidden guards, and civil officials rotated as night watch.

literal: Fengchen managed imperial supplies; the Three Shifts kept court order; hard stockades secured dawn and dusk.
idiomatic: Fengchen supplied the ruler, the Three Shifts kept assembly order, and hard stockades secured day and night.

literal: The regulations can be called strict indeed.
